name: windowing-pattern
context: A stream is unbounded, so no aggregate over 'everything' is computable. Windowing defines how records sharing a key are grouped into bounded regions of event time or record count so that aggregations and joins become well-defined: each record is assigned to one or more windows, the window accumulates state, a trigger decides when to emit, and a retention bound decides when the state can be discarded. Tumbling windows do not overlap, hopping and sliding windows overlap by a chosen advance, session windows are delimited by inactivity, and global windows span the whole stream.
benefits: Makes aggregation and join semantics well-defined on an unbounded input
Aligns computation with the business question — an hourly rate, a five-minute window, a rolling hour — instead of with batch boundaries
Enables parallel execution because a window's records share a key and therefore a partition
Explicit triggering and retention separate 'when do I emit' from 'when do I forget', which is what makes correct alerting possible
Continuous emission gives fresh partial results, while suppression converts the same computation into final results on demand
tradeoffs: Overlapping windows multiply state: a sliding window with a small advance can produce many concurrent windows per record
State for a window is retained until its end plus the allowed-lateness bound, so memory and storage lag the window boundary
Emitting final results requires a suppression buffer, which is unbounded unless explicitly capped
Continuous emission means downstream sees corrections; append-only sinks get duplicates and non-idempotent logic gets wrong answers
Wall-clock-aligned windows on event-time data produce the familiar repeated corrections at every hour boundary
use_cases: Per-minute and per-hour rate and count aggregation over high-volume event streams
Windowed joins where two streams are matched only when their records are close in event time
Alerts that must fire on a closed window rather than on every intermediate update
Sliding-window threshold detection for anomaly and compliance monitoring
Count windows over record counts rather than time, for fixed-size batching of unbounded input
avoid_when: The computation is a stateless per-record function — windows add state and cost for nothing
The input is bounded and complete, so ordinary batch grouping is simpler and exactly correct
Business semantics require whole-stream aggregation, which no finite window can provide
The output must be a single final number and no correction semantics are available downstream
component_types: Window assigner: maps each record to one or more windows (tumbling, hopping, sliding, session, global)
Window state store: per-key, per-window accumulator retained until the retention bound passes
Trigger: decides when a window fires — on element arrival, on a timer, or on both including merges
Grace or allowed lateness: the bound within which a late record still updates the window
Emit policy: continuous emission of partial results, or suppression until the window closes
Retention policy: when window state may be discarded
technology_stack: Apache Spark Structured Streaming (windowing and session window assignors)
anti_patterns: Emitting continuous results into an append-only sink, producing duplicate rows for the same window
Using a suppression buffer with no memory cap in production, turning a final-result feature into an OOM
Choosing a window size from a dashboard default rather than from the question being asked
Ignoring allowed lateness and treating a single firing as final
Windowing on wall-clock time while the data is event-time, guaranteeing boundary corrections
design_principles: Windows are the unit of aggregation because the stream has no end
Assignment, triggering and retention are three separate decisions
Every record belongs to a key and a window; both are part of the state identity
Emit partial results by default; suppress only when the business question needs a final answer
Bounds are explicit — grace, retention and state limits are stated, not defaulted
best_practices: Choose window size and advance from the question, then compute the resulting state volume before committing
Bound the suppression buffer explicitly in production code
Upsert by (key, window) downstream rather than appending
Set a grace period from measured lateness and log records discarded after it
Prefer tumbling windows unless overlap is genuinely required — hopping windows cost state per record
